newsitem.title: USA: Kemp-Gore debate 1996 U.S. election, and beyond.
newsitem.headline: Kemp-Gore debate 1996 U.S. election, and beyond.

text.p: The sparring by U.S. vice presidential rivals Al Gore and Jack Kemp over their running mates' policies is likely to have limited impact on the Nov. 5 election, but may offer a glimpse at the next White House race.

Throughout Wednesday night's 90-minute nationally televised affair, Republican Kemp gloated about the qualities and policies of Bob Dole, which he hoped will convince voters to make him president. Democrat Gore boasted that Clinton's record and his vision earned him a second term.

In an exchange devoid of stinging rhetoric and filled with a surprising amount of detail on relatively minor issues -- like creation of urban enterprise zones for Washington, D.C. and Los Angeles -- the two men touched on a broad range of subjects, from foreign policy to Medicare.

In one of the livelier exchanges, Kemp -- a long-time advocate for cutting taxes to spur economic growth -- hailed Dole's call for a 15 percent across-the-board tax cut. Glancing at Gore, Kemp said, "He'll call that trickle down, I'd call it Niagara Falls."

Gore replied: "The problem with this version of Niagara Falls is that Senator Dole and Mr. Kemp would put the American economy in a barrel and send it over the falls. It is a risky $550 billion tax scheme."

No matter who wins on Election Day, Kemp and Gore are virtually guaranteed of being crowned early frontrunners for their party's presidential nomination in the year 2000. President Bill Clinton has already said that, win or lose, this is his last race. Dole, at age 73, realistically is running his last race as well.

"This is probably a pretty good debate for Al Gore for the ... primaries in the Democratic party because he appealed to a liberal Democratic base," said John Buckley, the Dole campaign communications director, looking four years down the road. "It probably wasn't a very good job of appealing to most Americans."
Both Kemp and Gore dismissed any notion they were thinking about the future, insisting instead that their thoughts were focused only on the task at hand.

Gore has come up with a standard answer to deal with what he considers an awkward question about his future. "My top three political priorities are to re-elect Bill Clinton in 1996, to re-elect Bill Clinton in 1996 and to re-elect Bill Cinton in 1996." Kemp also brushes aside questions about his presidential aspirations.

However, there is something that speaks louder than the words of either man -- their actions. In 1988, the two men now fighting for the vice presidency tried hard but failed to win their parties' presidential nominations.

The vice presidency has been no sure stepping-stone to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, but it has been a step up for some. While the list of vice presidents includes names known only to scholars, like Thomas Marshall or Henry Wilson, it also contains the names of those who became recent presidents, like Harry Truman, Richard Nixon, Lyndon Johnson and George Bush.

In all, 14 vice presidents have gone on to become the nation's chief executive but few of them significantly influenced the elections when they were the vice presidential candidate. Democrats aggressively made Dan Quayle's qualifications an issue, but according to exit polls he had little to do with Bush's win in 1988 or his defeat in 1992.

Elijah Gosier, a St. Petersburg Times columnist, assessed the debate bluntly. "Most of us already know who will get our vote in November, and nothing anybody says -- especially two second bananas -- will change our minds."
"We're going to vote for Clinton, or we're going to vote for Dole," he said. "They could swap vice presidential running mates for all we care."
Gore and Kemp, of course, view it differently. They know their debate performances began ripples that may last four more years.
